title: C++ Versions: What Each Standard Added, from C++98 to C++26
summary: Walk C++ from C++98 to C++26: what each standard added and removed, how __cplusplus and feature-test macros say what you have, and why teams wait.
intro:
A video's benchmark has a loop that starts `for (auto trials{0uz}; ...)` and a constant named `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size`. Paste it into the sandbox and g++ 10.2 rejects both. The `uz` suffix arrived in C++23. The constant is C++17, a standard g++ 10.2 supports, yet its library only added that name in g++ 12. So the question "is this C++?" always has two more behind it: which C++, and which compiler?

This lesson walks the standards from C++98 to C++26: what each one added and removed, and which lesson of this course taught each piece. Then it shows how to find out what your own compiler has, with `__cplusplus`, feature-test macros, and the support tables. The sandbox runs everything through C++17 and much of C++20. This Mac's Apple clang 21 shows C++23 and C++26, built with `-std=c++23` and `-std=c++2c`, with the output it printed and the errors it gave.

steps.title: Standards, compilers, and __cplusplus
steps.body:
*From Source to Executable: Preprocess, Compile, Link* said that C++ is an ISO standard and that compilers implement it. Here is what that means.

The **standard** is a document, around 2,000 pages for C++23, that says what every piece of the language means and what the standard library must provide. It isn't software. It's written by **WG21**, the ISO committee for C++: a few hundred volunteers from compiler teams, chip makers, banks, game studios, and universities. A change starts as a numbered **paper**, like P2996 for reflection, and the committee votes papers in at its meetings, about three a year. Since C++11 it has run like a **train**: a new standard leaves every three years with whatever is ready, and a feature that isn't ready waits for the next one. Concepts missed C++11 and C++17 and arrived in C++20.

A compiler **implements** the standard, and so does its library: g++ with libstdc++, clang with libc++ on a Mac, and MSVC with Microsoft's own. Each adds features over several releases, so "supports C++20" arrives in pieces. g++ 10.2, the sandbox's, has all of C++17's language, nearly all of its library, and part of C++20. That lag is why most production code still targets C++17 or C++20. A project can use a feature only once every compiler that builds it has it: the g++ that a Linux server distribution keeps for years, a Mac, Windows, and the compilers of everyone who uses its library. So teams move one standard at a time, years after it's published.

`__cplusplus` holds the standard a file is being built as:

| Standard | `__cplusplus` | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C++98 | `199711L` | the first ISO standard |
| C++03 | `199711L` | bug fixes only, so the same number |
| C++11 | `201103L` | the big one |
| C++14 | `201402L` | plain `clang++` on this Mac |
| C++17 | `201703L` | this course |
| C++20 | `202002L` | g++ 10 says `201709L`, since its C++20 is unfinished |
| C++23 | `202302L` | the newest published standard |
| C++26 | `202400L` | a placeholder, until compilers take the finished standard's number |

You pick one with a flag. g++ and clang take `-std=c++17` or `-std=c++20`, or `-std=gnu++17`, the same plus GNU extensions. That's what g++ builds when you pass nothing: `gnu++14` for g++ 10, and `gnu++17` from g++ 11 on. MSVC takes `/std:c++17`, `/std:c++20`, or `/std:c++latest`, and it keeps `__cplusplus` at `199711L` unless you also pass `/Zc:__cplusplus`, putting the real value in its own `_MSVC_LANG`. This Mac, asked for each:

```text
$ for s in c++98 c++11 c++14 c++17 c++20 c++23 c++2c; do echo __cplusplus | clang++ -x c++ -std=$s -E -P -; done
199711L
201103L
201402L
201703L
202002L
202302L
202400L
```

Test the number with `>=`, never `==`. A newer standard only makes it bigger, the published C++26 will too, and g++ 10's `201709L` sits between C++17 and C++20, so an `==` test for either one fails there.

example.title: Which standards this build has
example.prompt: List every standard with yes or no, comparing __cplusplus with each standard's number, then name the newest this build has.
example.output:
__cplusplus: 201703
C++98: yes
C++11: yes
C++14: yes
C++17: yes
C++20: no
C++23: no
C++26 draft: no
newest: C++17
example.explanation:
Each entry pairs a name with the number `__cplusplus` takes when a file is built as that standard. `__cplusplus >= s.value` is true for every standard up to the one this build uses, so the loop prints yes through C++17 and leaves `newest` at the last yes. The sandbox builds C++17, `201703`. C++03 isn't in the table, since its number is C++98's.

The same file on this Mac prints yes on every line with `clang++ -std=c++2c`, ending `newest: C++26 draft`, and stops at `newest: C++14` with a plain `clang++`, the default *From Source to Executable: Preprocess, Compile, Link* warned about. `"C++26 draft"` is honest: `202400` is the placeholder that g++ and clang both use for C++26 until they take the finished standard's own number.

practice.title: A C++20 that isn't finished
practice.prompt:
Build the same report as C++20 in the sandbox, where g++ 10.2's unfinished C++20 gives a number between two standards.

1. The first line, `// -std=c++20`, is already there.
2. For each standard in `kStandards`, print its name, `: `, and `yes` when `__cplusplus >= value`, else `no`.
3. Print `newest: ` and the name of the last standard that printed yes.
4. Print `exact match: ` and `yes` if `__cplusplus` equals that standard's value, else `no`.

Expected output:

```text
__cplusplus: 201709
C++98: yes
C++11: yes
C++14: yes
C++17: yes
C++20: no
C++23: no
C++26 draft: no
newest: C++17
exact match: no
```

tests.output:
__cplusplus: 201709
C++98: yes
C++11: yes
C++14: yes
C++17: yes
C++20: no
C++23: no
C++26 draft: no
newest: C++17
exact match: no

hints: The loop is the example's: `const bool has = __cplusplus >= s.value;`, then print the name and yes or no.
Keep the value of the newest standard next to its name, in a `long newest_value` set at the same time as `newest`.
g++ 10.2 reports `201709` for C++20, which is above C++17's `201703`, so the last line is `exact match: no`.

steps.title: C++98, C++03, and C++11
steps.body:
**C++98**, the first ISO standard, wrote down what C++ had grown into since the 1980s: classes, templates, exceptions, namespaces, `std::string`, iostreams, and the **STL**, its containers, iterators, and algorithms. **C++03** fixed bugs in it, like what `T()` means for a plain struct, and nothing else. Eight quiet years followed, while a report called TR1 tried out `shared_ptr`, `unordered_map`, `<regex>`, and `<random>` in a namespace of their own, `std::tr1`.

**C++11**, called C++0x while it ran late, changed how C++ is written more than any standard since, so code from before 2011 can look like another language. Most of this course is C++11:

| C++11 added | In place of | Taught in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `auto` | spelling out `std::map<std::string, int>::const_iterator` | *Variables and Data Types* |
| range-for | an iterator loop | *Looping Over Arrays* |
| lambdas | a struct with an `operator()` | *Lambdas and STL Algorithms* |
| rvalue references and moves | copying a big object to hand it over | *Copy and Move Semantics* |
| `nullptr` | `NULL`, a macro for 0 | *Pointers* |
| `constexpr` | macros and constants worked out by hand | *const, constexpr, and Where a Value Lives* |
| `unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr` | a `delete` on every path out | *Smart Pointers: unique_ptr, shared_ptr, and weak_ptr* |
| `std::thread`, `std::atomic` | each OS's own thread API | *Threads, Data Races, and Mutexes*, later in the track |
| `<chrono>` | C's `time()`, in whole seconds | *Time in C++: chrono, Clocks, and Timestamps* |
| `enum class` | a plain `enum`, whose names leak out | *Switch, enum class, and the Ternary Operator* |
| braces and `std::initializer_list` | a `push_back` per element | *Initialization: Braces, Narrowing, and the Most Vexing Parse* |
| `override` and `final` | a typo that quietly made a new function | *Inheritance and Virtual Functions*, *Multiple Inheritance, the Diamond, and Virtual Bases* |
| variadic templates | an overload for each count of arguments | *Variadic Templates and Fold Expressions* |
| `static_assert` | tricks like an array of size -1 | *Compile-Time C++: constexpr, static_assert, and Type Traits* |

It added much more: `<cstdint>`, `std::array`, `std::unordered_map`, `std::function`, `<random>`, `= default` and `= delete`, `noexcept`, `decltype`, `using` aliases, raw strings, and the trailing return type, `auto f() -> int`. Under the threads sits the biggest change, the **memory model**. Before it, the standard didn't know threads existed, so what a data race even meant was up to each OS and compiler. *Atomics and Memory Ordering*, later in the track, works with that model.

C++11 also retired two things. It deprecated `std::auto_ptr`, C++98's smart pointer, whose copy quietly moved ownership away, in favor of `unique_ptr`. And its rules for `std::string` ruled out **copy-on-write**, where copies share one buffer until one of them writes. libstdc++ had used it, with a string of 8 bytes, a single pointer. Since g++ 5 it keeps short strings inside the object, the 32 bytes *std::string Essentials* measured, and the old layout survives only behind `_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0`, for programs that link against old libraries.

example.title: One task in two dialects
example.prompt: Count buys, total a position, own an order, and compare enums, each written once as C++98 and once as C++11.
example.explanation:
Each pair of lines does one job twice. `IsBuy` is the C++98 way to pass a test to `std::count_if`, a struct whose `operator()` holds it, and the lambda says the same in place. `net_98` spells out the iterator's type and walks it by hand, and `net_11` lets `auto` and range-for do both. The C++98 order needs its `delete`, while the `unique_ptr` deletes at the closing brace. Every pair prints the same, since C++11 changed how code reads, not what it does.

Built on this Mac with `clang++ -std=c++98`, the C++11 half mostly compiles anyway (some lines left out):

```text
dialects.cpp:24:16: warning: 'auto' type specifier is a C++11 extension [-Wc++11-extensions]
dialects.cpp:24:28: warning: range-based for loop is a C++11 extension [-Wc++11-extensions]
dialects.cpp:28:6: warning: scoped enumerations are a C++11 extension [-Wc++11-extensions]
dialects.cpp:36:28: error: non-aggregate type 'const std::vector<int>' cannot be initialized with an initializer list
dialects.cpp:38:64: warning: lambdas are a C++11 extension [-Wc++11-extensions]
7 warnings and 1 error generated.
```

That's the edge case: an older `-std` doesn't make clang forget newer features. It accepts most of them as **extensions**, with a warning, and only the braces fail. `-pedantic-errors` turns every warning like these into an error, 10 here, which is how a project makes sure its code really is the standard it names.

practice.title: Modernize two helpers
practice.prompt:
Rewrite two C++98 helpers in C++11 and check that each pair agrees.

1. Leave `IsSell`, `sells_98`, and `largest_98` as they are.
2. Make `fills11` hold the same four fills as `fills98`, written in braces.
3. Write `sells_11` with `std::count_if` and a lambda in place of `IsSell`.
4. Write `largest_11` with a range-for over `const auto&` entries: the largest quantity, or 0 when none is above 0.

Expected output:

```text
sells: 3 3
largest: 450 450
```
hints: Braces fill a vector in one line: `const std::vector<int> fills11 = {-40, 100, -60, -10};`.
The lambda replaces the struct: `std::count_if(fills.begin(), fills.end(), [](int qty) { return qty < 0; })`.
`for (const auto& entry : position)` gives each pair, and `entry.second` is its quantity.

steps.title: C++14, C++17, and what they removed
steps.body:
**C++14** finished what C++11 started, in small pieces:

- generic lambdas, `[](auto x) { ... }`, from *Variadic Templates and Fold Expressions*.
- return type deduction, `auto notional(long long q, long long px) { return q * px; }`.
- digit separators, `1'000'000`, from *Integer Types, sizeof, and Overflow*, and binary literals, `0b1010`, from *Numbers in Memory: Binary, Two's Complement, and IEEE 754*.
- `std::make_unique`, which C++11 forgot, from *Smart Pointers: unique_ptr, shared_ptr, and weak_ptr*.
- relaxed `constexpr`: C++11 allowed one `return` statement, and C++14 allows locals and loops, as in *Compile-Time C++: constexpr, static_assert, and Type Traits*.
- the literals `250ms`, from *Time in C++: chrono, Clocks, and Timestamps*, and `"abc"s` for a `std::string`.

**C++17**, this course's standard, added more:

- structured bindings (*Pairs, Tuples, and Structured Bindings*), `if constexpr` and class template argument deduction (*Templates: Writing Generic Code*), and `if` with an initializer (*If, Else If, and Else*).
- `std::optional` (*Infinity, Sentinels, and Null*), `std::variant` and `[[nodiscard]]` (*Errors in Fast Code: noexcept, Error Codes, and Results*), and `std::string_view` with `std::from_chars` (*`string_view` and Fast Parsing*).
- fold expressions (*Variadic Templates and Fold Expressions*), inline variables (*const, constexpr, and Where a Value Lives*), guaranteed copy elision (*Value Categories, std::move, and Copy Elision*), and `std::filesystem` (*Files: Streams, Buffers, and the Disk*).
- parallel algorithms, like `std::reduce(std::execution::par, ...)`, and `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size`, which *Tasks, Futures, and a Thread Pool* and *Memory Layout: Alignment, Padding, and Cache Lines* meet later in the track.

Those last two show what "supports C++17" can leave out. g++ 10.2 runs parallel algorithms on one thread unless Intel's TBB library is installed, and it has no `hardware_destructive_interference_size` at all, a name g++ added in version 12. Press Run for the error:

```cpp error
#include <iostream>
#include <new>

int main() {
    std::cout << std::hardware_destructive_interference_size << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

This Mac's libc++ has that constant, and no `std::execution::par`, unless you pass `-fexperimental-library`.

C++17 also **removed** things that earlier standards had deprecated:

| Removed in C++17 | Use instead | g++ 10.2 | Apple clang 21 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `std::auto_ptr` | `std::unique_ptr` | still there, with a warning | gone |
| `std::random_shuffle` | `std::shuffle` with an engine | still there | gone |
| `register` | nothing, the compiler picks registers | a warning | an error |
| trigraphs, like `??=` for `#` | the character itself | ignored, with a warning | ignored, with a warning |
| `throw(int)` after a function | `noexcept` | an error | an error |
| `++` on a `bool` | `= true` | an error | an error |

*Memory Hierarchy: Registers, Caches, RAM, Pages, and Disk* met `register`. The empty form, `throw()`, an old way to say `noexcept`, lasted until C++20, and both compilers still accept it even there. Compilers turn the language's removals into errors or warnings at once, but each library decides for itself: libstdc++ keeps `auto_ptr` and `random_shuffle` for old code, and libc++ drops them. Press Run for g++'s two errors:

```cpp error
void send() throw(int) {}  // a dynamic exception specification

int main() {
    bool armed = false;
    armed++;
    return 0;
}
```

example.title: A tour of C++14 and C++17
example.prompt: Use more than a dozen C++14 and C++17 features in one program, each marked with its standard.
example.output:
42 2.5 1000 10
1927500 1
AAPL=300 MSFT=-50 
qty 250
bad qty: 0
1 10 integer other
250
example.explanation:
Every line uses a C++14 or C++17 feature from the course. `twice` is one generic lambda called with an `int` and a `double`. `pow10(3)` runs its loop while compiling. `notional` deduces `long long` from its `return`. The structured bindings name each map entry's key and value, `parse_qty` returns an empty `std::optional` for `25x`, and the `if` declares `q` for its own test. `total` folds `+` over its pack, `kind` keeps only the `if constexpr` branch that fits its type, and `std::pair lot{kLot, 2.5}` deduces `std::pair<int, double>`.

Built on this Mac with `clang++ -std=c++14`, a pattern shows (some lines left out):

```text
tour.cpp:25:1: warning: inline variables are a C++17 extension [-Wc++17-extensions]
tour.cpp:28:37: warning: pack fold expression is a C++17 extension [-Wc++17-extensions]
tour.cpp:30:20: error: no template named 'optional' in namespace 'std'
tour.cpp:32:16: warning: decomposition declarations are a C++17 extension [-Wc++17-extensions]
tour.cpp:32:33: error: no member named 'from_chars' in namespace 'std'
tour.cpp:39:8: warning: constexpr if is a C++17 extension [-Wc++17-extensions]
tour.cpp:56:10: error: no member named 'variant' in namespace 'std'
6 warnings and 11 errors generated.
```

Newer **language** features compile with a warning, as extensions. Newer **library** names are errors, because libc++ declares them only when the standard is new enough.

practice.title: A quote report in C++17
practice.prompt:
Finish a quote report that uses one C++14 or C++17 feature per line.

1. Set `kMaxSpread` to 10000, written with a digit separator.
2. Make `all_positive` a fold expression that joins `(xs > 0)` with `&&`.
3. Make `spread` a generic lambda, with `auto` parameters, so it also works on `double`s.
4. Loop over `book` with structured bindings, `[symbol, quote]`, and print `symbol bid/ask spread n` for each, where `quote.first` is the bid and `quote.second` the ask.
5. For each token, use an `if` with an initializer to call `parse_px` and print `px ` and the price, or `px bad` when it's empty.

Expected output:

```text
max spread: 10000
all positive: 1 0
AAPL 19270/19280 spread 10
MSFT 41005/41010 spread 5
px 19275
px bad
spread as double: 0.25
```

tests.output:
max spread: 10000
all positive: 1 0
AAPL 19270/19280 spread 10
MSFT 41005/41010 spread 5
px 19275
px bad
spread as double: 0.25

hints: A fold with `&&` over a test is `return (... && (xs > 0));`, like the example's `(xs + ... + 0)`.
A generic lambda takes `auto` parameters: `[](auto bid, auto ask) { return ask - bid; }`.
`for (const auto& [symbol, quote] : book)` names both halves of each entry, and `if (const auto px = parse_px(token); px)` tests the optional it just made.

steps.title: C++20 to C++26, and feature tests

example.title: A feature report
example.prompt: Report which C++17 and C++20 features this build has from their feature-test macros, and pick a cache line constant with one.
example.output:
__cpp_structured_bindings: 201606
__cpp_lib_optional: 201606
__cpp_lib_filesystem: 201703
__cpp_concepts: missing
<format>: missing
cache line constant: 64, from our own
example.explanation:
Each `#ifdef` keeps one of its two lines before the compiler runs, so a missing feature prints `missing` instead of breaking the build. g++ 10.2 in C++17 mode has structured bindings, `std::optional`, and `std::filesystem` at their C++17 versions, and no concepts or `<format>`. `kLine` shows what a feature test is for: it uses the library's constant where the library has one and a constant of its own elsewhere, so the same file builds on both machines. Here that's 64, ours.

This Mac, `clang++ -std=c++17` and then `-std=c++23`:

```text
__cpp_structured_bindings: 202411
__cpp_lib_optional: 201606
__cpp_lib_filesystem: 201703
__cpp_concepts: missing
<format>: found
cache line constant: 256, from the library
```

```text
__cpp_structured_bindings: 202411
__cpp_lib_optional: 202110
__cpp_lib_filesystem: 201703
__cpp_concepts: 202002
<format>: found
cache line constant: 256, from the library
```

Two surprises. clang reports `__cpp_structured_bindings` as `202411`, a C++26 addition it already has, even in C++17 mode, so a language macro can report a newer version than the standard you asked for. And `__has_include(<format>)` is true under C++17, as *The Preprocessor: Macros and Conditional Compilation* warned, though `std::format` needs C++20. The library's `256` is the next lesson's subject.

practice.title: A C++20 feature report
practice.prompt:
Build a feature report as C++20 in the sandbox, and let a feature test choose how to count bits.

1. When `__cpp_lib_bitops` is defined, `bits` returns `std::popcount(x)` and `kBitsFrom` is `"std::popcount"`. Otherwise `bits` counts the 1 bits in a loop and `kBitsFrom` is `"a loop"`.
2. Print `__cpp_concepts`, `__cpp_lib_span`, and `__cpp_lib_format`, each as `name: value`, or `name: missing` when it isn't defined.
3. Print `<format>: found` or `<format>: missing`, using `__has_include`.
4. The first and last lines are already printed.

Expected output:

```text
__cplusplus: 201709
__cpp_concepts: 201907
__cpp_lib_span: 202002
__cpp_lib_format: missing
<format>: missing
bits in 11: 3, from std::popcount
```

tests.output:
__cplusplus: 201709
__cpp_concepts: 201907
__cpp_lib_span: 202002
__cpp_lib_format: missing
<format>: missing
bits in 11: 3, from std::popcount

hints: Each macro is an `#ifdef __cpp_concepts` with a print of its value, then `#else` and a print of `missing`, then `#endif`.
`#if defined(__cpp_lib_bitops)` goes around a whole function: one `bits` with `std::popcount`, and after `#else`, one with a loop.
g++ 10.2 has `<bit>` and concepts in C++20 mode, but no `<format>`, so the last lines are `missing`, `missing`, and `std::popcount`.

recap:
- WG21, the ISO committee, has published a standard every three years since C++11, and a feature that isn't ready waits for the next one. Compilers and their libraries implement each one over several releases.
- `__cplusplus` is `199711` for C++98 and C++03, then `201103`, `201402`, `201703`, `202002`, `202302`, and the C++26 draft's `202400`. Compare it with `>=`. Pick a standard with `-std=c++17`, or `/std:c++17` and `/Zc:__cplusplus` with MSVC.
- C++11 is the big one: `auto`, range-for, lambdas, moves, `nullptr`, `constexpr`, smart pointers, threads and the memory model, `<chrono>`, `enum class`, braces, `override`, variadic templates, and `static_assert`.
- C++14 rounded it off: generic lambdas, deduced return types, `1'000'000`, `0b1010`, and `make_unique`. C++17 added structured bindings, `if constexpr`, `optional`, `variant`, `string_view`, `filesystem`, folds, `[[nodiscard]]`, and inline variables.
- C++17 removed `auto_ptr`, `random_shuffle`, `register`, trigraphs, `throw(X)`, and `bool++`. A library may keep a removed name, the language doesn't.
- An older `-std` accepts many newer language features with a warning but hides newer library names. `-pedantic-errors` makes the warnings errors.
- C++23 adds `std::print`, `std::expected`, `std::mdspan`, `uz`, `if consteval`, and deducing this. C++26, finished in 2026 but not yet published, adds reflection, contracts, `std::execution`, `std::inplace_vector`, and `#embed`. This Mac has its small pieces only.
- Feature-test macros (`__cpp_...`, `__cpp_lib_...`, `<version>`) and `__has_include` say what this compiler has. cppreference's compiler support page says which compilers have it.

Next, **Where a Feature Comes From: Standard, Compiler, OS, Hardware** takes the video's snippet apart by origin: the language, the library, the choices each implementation makes, the OS, the hardware, and one compiler's extensions.
